lines.text: Student life in Britain is about far more than lectures and exams — it is a formative period of independence, friendship, and self-discovery. Most first-year students live in halls of residence, sharing kitchens and communal spaces with flatmates from diverse backgrounds. Learning to cook, do laundry, manage a budget, and coexist with strangers are essential life skills developed during this time. The students' union (SU) is the social heart of university life, hosting hundreds of clubs and societies — from drama and debating to sports teams and cultural groups. Joining societies is considered vital for making friends, developing skills, and building a CV. Part-time work is common: students work in cafés, shops, bars, and tutoring to supplement their maintenance loans. Budgeting is a constant challenge — balancing rent, food, transport, textbooks, and social activities on limited income. Student discounts (via NUS cards or student ID) help stretch budgets at shops, cinemas, and restaurants. Mental health awareness has become central to student welfare: universities now offer counselling services, mental health advisors, and peer support networks. The academic-social balance is a defining challenge — too much socialising risks academic failure; too much study risks isolation and burnout. Graduation — the ceremony where degrees are formally awarded — marks the transition from student to graduate, celebrated with cap and gown, photographs, and family pride.

lines.text: 'Freshers' flu' is the illness many first-year students catch in their first weeks — a combination of stress, late nights, shared living spaces, and new germs. It's so common it has its own name and is a rite-of-passage joke among British students.

lines.text: UK student loans work uniquely: you repay only when earning above a threshold (currently £25,000+), at 9% of income above that. After 40 years, remaining debt is written off. 'Plan 5', 'repayment threshold', and 'student debt' are terms every graduate knows.

lines.text: Taking a 'gap year' between school and university is a distinctly British tradition. Students travel, volunteer, or work — gaining life experience. 'Gap yah' (mocking pronunciation) became a comedy sketch highlighting privileged gap-year travel stories.

lines.text: Historically, the 'milk round' was when major employers visited universities to recruit graduates — named after the milkman's regular route. Now mostly online ('virtual milk round'), the term persists: 'Are you doing the milk round?' means 'Are you applying to graduate schemes?'
